newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends higher in mostly technical U.S. trade.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends higher in mostly technical U.S. trade.

text.p: The dollar ended higher in technically-driven U.S. trade, with traders adjusting from earlier selling versus yen after Japan's trade surplus jumped.

Short-covering also lifted the dollar against the mark, amid signs that European Economic and Moneteary Union (EMU) is moving forward in the wake of the Amsterdam summit, despite big questions about key nations cutting budget deficits enough to ensure a strong start to the euro.
"It really seems to be traders' postions driving what's going on over last 24 hours," said Rick Gomes, a managing director at Republic National Bank of New York.
The dollar recovered in the U.S. after dipping under 113 yen when Japan reported that its trade surplus swelled 222 percent, to 738 billion yen, in May from a year earlier.

The dollar ended near its high at 113.60/70 yen, up from 113.10/20 at the open. It also sprang back from an overnight low of 1.7225 marks, ending at 1.7335/45 marks, up from an opening quote of 1.7267/70.

Orders from both buyers and sellers were reported to be stacked near 113.20 yen in the U.S session. Traders said there was good buying interest between 113.10 and 112.50 yen from Japanese institutions during the overnight session.
Japan's surplus met the very upper end of expectations, but traders used the quick decline to book profits before data on the U.S. trade deficit on Thursday.

Japan's surplus with the United States rose 93 percent, and came one day before the U.S. Commerce Department releases international trade figures, which are expected confirm a deterioration in the U.S. trade position.

"People were genuinely interested to sell," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd. "But maybe people realized we still have Thursday's U.S. trade number and that is expected to reconfirm the (Japan) trade surplus is huge."
Economists expect the U.S. trade deficit, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Thursday, to have widened to $10.0 billion in April, following at $8.51 billion gap in March.

Some U.S. businesses and economists have blamed the the dollar's rise against the yen in 1996 and 1997 for making U.S. exports to Japan more expensive while making Japanese products in the U.S. irresistably cheap.
Few expect the Japanese trade surplus to be the primary topic of discussion at the weekend summit meeting of the Group of Seven big industrial nations in Denver.
But trade issues are expected to come up in one-on-one talks between Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Denver.
"Nobody expects anything special to come out of it regarding foreign exchange but one always has to be cautious," Yu said.
Dollar/mark, meanwhile, was still mulling EMU issues.
"The tug and pull on dollar/marks remains based on whatever you believe the appropriate EMU scenario is going to be," said Rick Gomes, managing director at Republic National Bank of New York.

On Wednesday, the U.K.'s daily Financial Times reported the French deficit is set to exceed by at least half a percentage point the requirement that states wishing to qualify for the single currency must have deficits not larger than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.

Also, Belgium said it would sell gold reserves in the form of commemorative coins to reduce the country's debt, which boosted the dollar on fears that one-time budget measures mean the mark would be supplanted with a weak euro.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4470/80 Swiss from 1.4445/55 and to Canadian $1.3930/35 from C$1.3865/70.
The pound was unchanged at $1.6380/90 and the Australian dollar fell to $0.7484/89 from $0.7515/20.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
